newsitem.title: USA: U.S. campaign scandal may complicate China WTO bid.
newsitem.headline: U.S. campaign scandal may complicate China WTO bid.

text.p: China's alleged effort to funnel money into U.S. election campaigns may give a boost to an effort in Congress to ensure lawmakers have a say in Beijing's bid to join the World Trade Organisation, trade analysts said.

House Democratic Leader Richard Gephardt plans to introduce legislation that would require a congressional vote on U.S. approval of China's entry into the World Trade Organisation, according to an aide.

It is the same bill the Missouri Democrat supported last year and some trade analysts believe it could gain broad support in light of recent allegations that China may have tried to make illegal contributions in the 1996 election campaign. China has strongly denied the reports.

Gephardt, a potential rival to Vice President Al Gore for the Democratic presidential nomination in the 2000 election campaign who has staked out a get-tough position on trade supported by organised labour, hopes to get good support from both Democrats and Republicans, an aide said.
The proposed legislation would ensure that Congress is able to exercise its constitutional authority over international trade, the aide said.

The White House has argued that the legislation is not needed because of ongoing consultations with Congress on the the issue. But analysts said a vote for the bill may be irresistible to lawmakers who want to take a tough line on China, but who may be reluctant to support a more blunt effort by conservative and liberal groups to withdraw China's Most Favoured Nation trading privileges.

"This gives members a chance to show that they don't like suppression of human rights and believe China is a bit of a rogue in the international community," said Bill Frenzel, a former Republican member of Congress who is now with the Brookings Institution think tank.

"There are a lot of members on both sides of the aisle who have expressed interest in this issue before," said Greg Mastel, trade analyst with the Economic Strategy Institute, a Washington think tank.
He suggested that the administration may be in no position to fight the Gephardt bill because of the campaign fund-raising scandal engulfing the White House.

"It's the kind of issue where because of the political sensitivities unique to the situation and because of the larger issue of Congress' involvement in trade, it might be hard for the administration to resist," he said.

Robert Lighthizer, a Washington trade lawyer who advised unsuccessful Republican presidential candidate Bob Dole during the 1996 campaign, wrote a recent column for the New York Times urging a greater say by Congress on China's WTO bid in light of allegations about possible illegal campaign contributions to the Democratic National Committee from Asian sources.

He suggested the money was meant to influence U.S. policy on China's WTO bid and said a decision shared with Congress would assure Americans that "their vital economic interests will not suffer because certain politicians in Washington accepted money from foreign interests with a very foreign agenda."

Negotiations with China on its bid to join the Geneva-based trading body have shifted into high gear in recent weeks with a new offer from Beijing to drop trade barriers and bring its trading rules in line with the global trading system.

Jeffrey Schott, a senior trade analyst at the Institute for International Economics, said the United States by itself could not block China's entry into the WTO but it could make negotiations with Beijing more difficult.
"It certainly would complicate the negotiations," he said.
